summary: Defines a URN namespace for the GSMA and a namespace-specific string for the IMEI, which identifies mobile equipment in GSM, UMTS, and LTE networks. It also covers the IMEISV. These URNs nearly always contain personal information and must be handled with care.

plainLanguage.summary: Every mobile phone carries a fifteen-digit number that identifies the handset to the cellular network. RFC 7254 gives that number a standard written form, so that an Internet protocol which needs to name a device can write it the same way everyone else does. It also spells out the privacy rules, because the number points at a person's handset.

questions: how to write imei as urn
subtitle: A standard web-style name for the serial number that identifies a mobile phone.

tldr.problem: Every mobile phone has a fifteen-digit serial number that cellular networks use to identify it, but Internet protocols that need to name a device have no agreed way to write it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves a Uniform Resource Name namespace for the mobile industry and defines how the device identifier is written inside it, with an optional parameter for the software version.
tldr.outcome: The document warns that these names are personal information and must be handled carefully. It says they must not be used as a password, as a user address, or in messages meant to be anonymous.

today: RFC 7254 is an Informational RFC published in May 2014, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The namespace it defines is registered with IANA and maintained by the mobile industry association, which may add further identifiers under it in future.

sections.title: What the Document Defines
sections.content:
The document defines a Uniform Resource Name namespace for the Global System for Mobile Communications Association and a namespace specific string for the International Mobile station Equipment Identity, together with an associated parameter for the International Mobile station Equipment Identity and Software Version number, following the namespace registration requirements of the URN rules.

The namespace identifier is gsma, for identities used in GSM, Universal Mobile Telecommunications System and Long Term Evolution networks. The device identifiers are managed by the association, so the namespace is managed by it too. Only the imei string is defined under the gsma namespace at present, though the association may define others later through future Informational RFCs.

The IMEI is 15 decimal digits long: a type allocation code of 8 digits, a serial number of 6 digits, and one spare digit. The type allocation code identifies the type of the mobile equipment, and is chosen from a range of values allocated to the manufacturer in order to identify the model uniquely. The serial number is an individual number that identifies each device within that code. The spare digit is used as a check digit to validate the whole number, and is always set to zero when the equipment transmits it. The IMEISV is 16 digits long: the same code and serial number, plus a two-digit software version number allocated by the manufacturer.

The information here is meant to be a concise guide for anyone wishing to use the two identifiers as URNs. Nothing in the document overrides the 3GPP specification that actually defines them. The association itself is a global trade association representing nearly 800 mobile phone operators across 220 territories and countries.
sections.plainLanguage: The number is not one piece. The first eight digits say what model of handset it is, the next six say which one, and the last digit is a checksum that catches typing mistakes.

sections.title: How the Name Is Written
sections.content:
The identifier is written in ASCII characters with a hierarchical structure expressed in Augmented Backus-Naur Form. The overall shape is urn: followed by the namespace identifier, a colon, and the namespace specific string. The namespace specific string is either the imei specifier or a future specifier. The imei specifier is the word imei, a colon, and then either the ordinary value or an extended value, optionally followed by a software version parameter and then optionally an IMEI version parameter.

The ordinary value is three fields separated by hyphens: the type allocation code of eight digits, the serial number of six digits, and the spare digit. The software version parameter is svn= followed by two digits, and the IMEI version parameter is vers= followed by one digit. The future specifier and the extended value are left for the association to define, within the character set allowed, which is letters, digits and the characters hyphen, full stop, underscore, per cent sign and colon.

Two examples are given. The first is an ordinary identifier with the version parameter set to zero: urn:gsma:imei:90420156-025763-0;vers=0. The second is the same device with a software version appended, in which case the spare digit is set to zero: urn:gsma:imei:90420156-025763-0;svn=42.
sections.plainLanguage: The written form is ordinary: a prefix saying whose number it is, the three groups of digits separated by hyphens, and any extra information after a semicolon.

sections.title: Versioning, Equivalence and Validation
sections.content:
The optional version parameter and the extended value are there for extensibility. If the format of the identifier were ever extended, with more digits or with hexadecimal digits for instance, the version parameter would carry a non-zero value and the extended value would be defined to describe the new syntax. A version of zero, or no version parameter at all, means the name is compliant with the format given here. Any change to the format needs the same process used for adding or changing a namespace specific string, which is publication of a future Informational RFC approved by IETF consensus.

The version parameter was chosen instead of defining a second namespace specific string, such as imei2, because many applications will do nothing more than compare the ordinary value as a string. Even if the format or the length of that value changes later, those applications should keep working without being updated to understand a new name.

Two GSMA IMEI names are equivalent when they have the same ordinary value and the same parameter values in the same order, except that a version parameter of zero is ignored for comparison. All such comparisons are case insensitive. The identifier can be validated using the mechanism in the 3GPP specification, but there is no mechanism for validating the software version field. The namespace is global in scope, and it is not currently globally resolvable, so the question of how to resolve a name to a resource does not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: If the format of these numbers ever changes, the same name keeps working, with a version number saying which format is in use. That way old software does not break.

sections.title: The Two Number Formats
sections.content:
When the IMEI travels inside a cellular signalling message it is 15 decimal digits encoded in 8 octets using Binary Coded Decimal, as defined in the 3GPP signalling specification. The figure in the RFC is an abstract representation; the actual storage format in memory is implementation specific. In that representation the most significant digit of the type allocation code sits in the least significant bits of the first octet, the most significant digit of the serial number in the least significant bits of the fifth octet, and the spare digit in the least significant bits of the eighth octet.

The spare digit is a single decimal digit. When the IMEI is stored on the equipment and in network equipment it holds a value used as a check digit, intended to avoid manual reporting errors, such as when a customer registers a stolen phone at the operator's customer care desk, and to help guard against incorrect entries being provisioned into the network. It is always set to zero when the equipment transmits it, including in the URN form. The 3GPP specification gives a mechanism for computing the actual check digit in order to validate the code and the serial number.

The IMEISV is 16 decimal digits in 8 octets, also Binary Coded Decimal. Its type allocation code and serial number are the same as for the IMEI, and it adds a software version number allocated by the manufacturer. In its octet representation the most significant digit of the code sits in the most significant bits of the first octet, the serial number in the most significant bits of the fifth, and the software version in the most significant bits of the eighth.
sections.plainLanguage: On the air, these numbers are packed two digits to a byte. The check digit is filled in when the number is stored and sent as a zero, which is why the written form normally ends in a zero.

sections.title: Why the Internet Needs This
sections.content:
Mobile devices interoperate with Internet devices for voice and data services, and to do that they need Internet protocols that work end to end between devices in the cellular networks and devices in the general internet. Some of those protocols require URNs as identifiers. Within the cellular networks, devices are identified by their IMEI or IMEISV, and internet users need to be able to receive and include the name in various protocol elements. The namespace therefore has to be registered with IANA, to guarantee uniqueness and to prevent conflicts both inside the internet and inside the cellular networks.

The reverse is also true. Internet implementations will not generally hold IMEI identifiers, and the identifiers they generate will typically be URNs in other namespaces or, depending on the context, may not be URNs at all. Implementations are advised to be ready to process names other than those in the gsma namespace, so that they interoperate.

A URN was chosen as the most appropriate kind of name, because these identifiers are used and transported much like the Universally Unique Identifier, which is itself defined as a URN. Because the specifications of protocols that carry device identifiers often require the identifier to be globally unique and in URN form, the URN formats for these two identifiers had to be defined. IANA has registered the formal URN namespace gsma in the registry of Uniform Resource Name namespaces, using the registration template given in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone on a cellular network and a server on the internet sometimes need to refer to the same device, so both have to agree on how the device is named. Registering the name with IANA is what stops two different industries inventing the same one.

sections.title: Privacy Rules for These Names
sections.content:
IMEIs, with the spare value set to the check digit, are displayable on most mobile devices and in many cases are printed on the case inside the battery compartment. Anyone with brief physical access to the device can easily obtain the IMEI. The document is therefore emphatic that IMEIs must not be used as security capabilities, that is, as identifiers whose mere possession grants access. Unfortunately there are currently examples of applications that use the IMEI for authorisation, and some service providers' customer service departments have been known to treat knowledge of the IMEI as proof that the caller is the legitimate owner of the handset. Both are inappropriate uses.

The software version identifies only the lower-layer software that has passed certification testing, not the operating system or the applications, but it could still identify software known to be vulnerable. The IMEISV must therefore be delivered only to trusted entities inside carrier networks and not to the internet at large, and must not be delivered to devices that are not trusted. This is a similar concern to the one about the User-Agent header in SIP.

IMEIs are almost always personally identifiable information, so these names must be treated as such in all cases. The IMEI name must not be included in messages intended to convey any level of anonymity. Because the IMEI is permanently assigned to the device and does not change when ownership changes, even across a complete software reload, the IMEI name must not be used as a user identifier or a user address by an application, since that would let the new owner of a device receive the previous owner's traffic or reach the previous owner's services. The identifier could also be used to track people if sent in the clear. Uses of the IMEI name with IETF protocols require a specification and IETF Expert Review, protocols carrying it should at a minimum use channels that are strongly encrypted hop by hop, and end-to-end encryption is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone holding a phone can read its number off the screen. So it must never be treated as a secret, never used to stand for a user, and never sent where it is not needed.

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF THE TWO NUMBERS

cells: The model of the equipment, from a range allocated to the manufacturer
The individual device within that model
A check digit, sent as zero and used to catch typing errors
The software version, in the IMEISV only

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR HANDLING THESE NAMES

items.title: Never a password
items.text: The number is readable by anyone holding the phone, so it must not grant access.

items.title: Not a user address
items.text: It belongs to the device, not the person, and does not change when the phone is sold.

items.title: Personal data
items.text: Treat these names as personally identifiable information in every case.

items.title: Keep the version inside the carrier
items.text: The software version may reveal a vulnerable release, so it must not go out to the internet.

items.title: Encrypt the channel
items.text: Send it over a channel that is encrypted hop by hop, and end to end where possible.
